text.p: German drugs group Schering AG on Monday said nine-month profits jumped 66 percent, proving business was back on track and could set a new record for 1996 just months after a string of serious problems.
Schering chief executive Giuseppe Vita, clearly pleased that results topped forecasts, said net profit climbed to 286 million marks ($190 million) while sales climbed 12 percent to 3.85 billion.
"Who would have dreamt a year ago that Schering would already be able to present such a pleasing nine-month profit today -- the numbers top even our own expectations," Vita told a news conference.

Noting that similarly strong first-half results were not a fluke, Schering chief financial officer Klaus Pohle told a news conference 1996 profits will show a 34 percent rise from 249 million marks, when currency turmoil seriously dented results.
Full year sales at the world's largest maker of oral contraceptives are expected to top 5.2 billion marks.
Shareholders too will profit from the recovery as the board plans to raise this year's dividend payout to two marks per share from 1.55 marks paid out for 1995, Pohle said.

But Schering also warned against an overly optimistic outlook saying profits would have risen only 34 percent on an adjusted basis since the group took a huge writedown last year after it pulled its new x-ray drug Isovist 280 off the market.
Schering shares were up 1.48 percent at 126.70 marks in late afternoon trading, having set a year high in early trade.
For 1997, Pohl sees profits growing in single digit percentage point rates with sales totalling 5.9 billion marks.

Analysts, welcoming nine month data, said Schering's outlook was slightly disappointing. "I think the group was a bit conservative for next year," said Markus Rausch analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.

Pohle explained Schering will face costs of some 70 million marks next year for its acquisitions, Jenapharma and Leiras, and analysts added the group may fear another bout of currency trouble or a softer rise in volume sales.
In the first nine months, volume sales, rising 12 percent, and stabler currency relations were instrumental to growth with multiple-sclerosis drug Betaferon contributing strong sales.
"We generate our profits largely abroad," Pohle said, adding sales in Latin America, the United States, Schering's largest single market, and southern Europe led the way.
Additionally Schering also benefited from the stronger dollar leaving only the yen a sore spot, the group said.

Among its three key business areas, sales in diagnostics, largely x-ray media, rose one percent to 1.2 billion which Pohle said was due to aggressive price cuts in Japan and the United States which had curbed results.

Meanwhile therapeutics, which includes Betaferon, jumped 15 percent to one billion marks and fertility and hormone therapy rose 11 percent to 1.17 billion marks, showing last's years pill scare barely impacted results this year.
Pohle said the group had been able to compensate a six percent sales drop in birth control pill Femovan sales as women switched back to Schering's other pills.
Medical researchers alleged third generation pills like Femovan raise the chance of thrombosis prompting German health authorities to restrict prescriptions last year.

Betaferon sales climbed by 36 percent to nearly 400 million marks leaving Schering confident it can still reach its full year sales target of 535 million marks, trimmed back from 600 million marks after the launch in Europe proved difficult.

"We stick by our sales target and expect we can catch up now that France has agreed the pricing issue," Pohle said. Sales in the U.K., where insurance companies failed to free up funds for the expensive treatment, remain disappointing.
In the United States, where the drug is called Betaseron and has enjoyed several years of unrivalled sales, Schering said it was feeling the launch of rival Biogen's Avonex product.
But Vita remained optimistic that patients who switched to Avonex complaining of flu-like side effects with Betaseron will soon return as Avonex's dosage is weaker.
Meanwhile Schering also said crop protection unit AgrEvo's results were pleasing but that a one billion mark acquisition would push back the unit's bourse listing to 2000.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($1=1.5033 Mark)
